title: England Has a Private School Problem
author: Jared Cooney Horvath
summary: Jared Cooney Horvath tests his own case against classroom EdTech against England's celebrated PISA result, asking how the UK reached the global top ten if technology undermines learning. He notes that the rise is largely relative, since reading is flat and maths slipping while other systems fall further. Using PISA's technology-use index, he shows that the UK increased classroom technology use far less than the average of 31 other systems, and that England outperformed Scotland, which adopted more technology and declined faster. The surprise comes from splitting England's sectors: fee-paying independent schools raised their tech index sharply and saw SES-adjusted achievement fall, while state schools barely raised theirs and improved. He is careful to say these observational patterns do not prove causation. His message is one of caution, given £900 million in annual EdTech spending and near-universal access: England is the barrier at the top of the cliff, and greater use is a choice, not an inevitability.
points: England's top-ten PISA ranking reflects other systems sliding rather than a sustained rise in its own scores, which is why Horvath treats it as a test case for his thesis.
Across 32 systems, the UK's classroom technology use grew only 0.30 points versus a 0.95 average elsewhere, and it was the only system to show gains in maths, reading and science.
England's rising technology index of 0.29 and rising achievement contrasts with Scotland's faster technology growth and a much steeper decline.
Within England, independent schools raised technology use by 1.35 points while achievement fell, whereas state schools raised it by 0.19 while achievement improved.
With £900 million a year in EdTech spending and 98 percent of state pupils having access, restraint is a choice England must keep making.
quotes: Stand still long enough while everyone else slides backwards, and it appears as though you’re racing ahead.

To be fair, holding steady while many other countries decline is no small feat — but it raises an important challenge to the central argument against classroom EdTech: if classroom technology is undermining learning around the world, how has the UK managed to avoid the worst of it?
Across the other 31 systems, the average increase was 0.95 points (from 1.90 to 2.85), roughly three times larger.
Put simply, Scotland combined faster growth in classroom technology use with a markedly less favorable achievement trajectory than England.

By no means does this comparison establish that technology caused the divergence. Other differences — including the countries’ contrasting approaches to curriculum and teaching — almost certainly play a role.
In short, the sector that embraced technology more declined, while the sector that embraced it less improved.
According to the British Government, the UK spends £900 million per year on EdTech, making it the largest EdTech sector in Europe.
In England, I feel more like the barrier at the top of the cliff. Despite having the infrastructure in place, state schools have yet to drive over the edge.
But they offer no reason to assume that following independent schools toward greater screen use will improve learning. Alongside the wider evidence base, this gives England good reason to pause.
